paragraphs: It is remarkable that in every case ancient history reports in which a government was established by deliberate and common consent, the task of framing it was not given to an assembly of men. It was carried out by some individual citizen of outstanding wisdom and proven integrity.

We learn that Minos was the first founder of the government of Crete, and Zaleucus of that of the Locrians. Theseus first, and then Draco and Solon, set up the government of Athens. Lycurgus was the lawgiver of Sparta. Romulus laid the foundation of the original government of Rome, and two of his elected successors, Numa and Tullius Hostilius, completed the work. When the monarchy was abolished, Brutus put the consular administration in its place. He came forward with a plan for such a reform, which, he claimed, Tullius Hostilius had prepared, and his skill won for it the assent and ratification of the senate and the people. The same holds true of confederate governments. Amphictyon, we are told, was the author of the one that bore his name. The Achaean league was first born through Achaeus and born a second time through Aratus.

In every instance we cannot determine what part these reputed lawgivers played in their respective establishments, or how far they held the lawful authority of the people. In some cases, however, the proceeding was strictly regular. Draco appears to have been entrusted by the people of Athens with unlimited powers to reform their government and laws. And Solon, according to Plutarch, was in a manner compelled by the universal vote of his fellow citizens to take on himself the sole and absolute power of remodeling the constitution. The proceedings under Lycurgus were less regular. But so far as the advocates of a regular reform could prevail, they all looked to the individual efforts of that celebrated patriot and sage, instead of trying to bring about a revolution through a deliberative body of citizens.

Where could it have come from that a people as jealous of their liberty as the Greeks were should abandon caution so far as to place their destiny in the hands of a single citizen? Where could it have come from that the Athenians, who would not allow an army to be commanded by fewer than ten generals, and who needed no other proof of danger to their liberties than the illustrious merit of a fellow citizen, should consider one illustrious citizen a better keeper of their own fortunes and their posterity's than a select body of citizens, from whose joint deliberations more wisdom and more safety might have been expected? These questions cannot be fully answered without supposing that the fear of discord and disunion among a number of counselors outweighed their fear of treachery or incapacity in a single individual. History also tells us of the difficulties these celebrated reformers had to contend with, and of the expedients they were forced to use to put their reforms into effect. Solon, who seems to have followed a more temporizing policy, confessed that he had not given his countrymen the government best suited to their happiness, but the one most tolerable to their prejudices. And Lycurgus, who held more firmly to his object, had to mix some violence with the authority of superstition, and secured his final success by a voluntary renunciation, first of his country and then of his life. These lessons teach us, on the one hand, to admire the improvement America has made on the ancient way of preparing and establishing regular plans of government. On the other hand, they serve no less to warn us of the hazards and difficulties that go with such experiments, and of the great imprudence of multiplying them without need.

Is it an unreasonable conjecture that whatever errors the plan of the Convention contains are such as have resulted from lack of earlier experience in this complicated and difficult subject, rather than from any lack of accuracy or care in investigating it, and consequently are such as will not be found until an actual trial has pointed them out? Many considerations of a general nature make this conjecture probable, and so does the particular case of the Articles of Confederation. Notice that when these articles were submitted to the individual States for ratification, they produced numerous objections and proposed amendments. Not one of them alludes to the great and radical error that actual trial has since uncovered. If we except the observations that New Jersey was led to make by her local situation rather than by any special foresight, it may be doubted whether a single suggestion was weighty enough to justify revising the system. There is nevertheless abundant reason to suppose that, trivial as these objections were, some States would have clung to them with very dangerous inflexibility, had their zeal for their opinions and supposed interests not been stifled by the more powerful feeling of self-preservation. We may remember that one State persisted for several years in refusing her agreement, although the enemy remained the whole time at our gates, or rather in the very bowels of our country. In the end she was brought around by no weaker motive than the fear of being blamed for prolonging the public calamities and endangering the outcome of the contest. Every fair-minded reader will draw the proper reflections from these important facts.

A patient finds his disorder growing worse every day, and that an effective remedy cannot be delayed any longer without extreme danger. After coolly considering his situation and the characters of different physicians, he picks and calls in those he judges most capable of relieving him and most deserving of his confidence. The physicians attend. His case is carefully examined and a consultation is held. They agree unanimously that the symptoms are critical, but that with proper and timely relief the case is so far from desperate that it may even lead to an improvement of his constitution. They are equally unanimous in prescribing the remedy by which this happy effect is to be produced. But no sooner is the prescription made known than a number of people step in. Without denying that the disorder is real or dangerous, they assure the patient that the prescription will be poison to his constitution, and forbid him, on pain of certain death, to use it. Might not the patient reasonably demand, before he ventured to follow this advice, that the authors of it should at least agree among themselves on some other remedy to take its place? And if he found them differing as much from one another as from his first counselors, would he not act prudently in trying the experiment those first counselors unanimously recommended, rather than listening to people who could neither deny the need of a speedy remedy nor agree in proposing one?

America at this moment is such a patient in such a situation. She has been aware of her malady. She has obtained regular and unanimous advice from men of her own careful choosing. And others warn her against following this advice, on pain of the most fatal consequences. Do the advisers deny that her danger is real? No. Do they deny the need of some speedy and powerful remedy? No. Are they agreed, are even any two of them agreed, in their objections to the proposed remedy or in the proper one to put in its place? Let them speak for themselves. This one tells us that the proposed Constitution ought to be rejected because it is not a confederation of the States but a government over individuals. Another admits that it ought to be a government over individuals to a certain extent, but by no means to the extent proposed. A third does not object to a government over individuals, or to the extent proposed, but to the lack of a bill of rights. A fourth agrees that a bill of rights is absolutely necessary, but argues that it ought to declare, not the personal rights of individuals, but the rights reserved to the States in their political capacity. A fifth is of the opinion that a bill of rights of any sort would be superfluous and out of place, and that the plan would be beyond objection but for the fatal power of regulating the times and places of election. An objector in a large State cries out loudly against the unreasonable equality of representation in the Senate. An objector in a small State is equally loud against the dangerous inequality in the House of Representatives. From one quarter we are alarmed at the amazing expense, owing to the number of persons who are to run the new government. From another quarter, and sometimes from the same quarter on another occasion, the cry is that Congress will be only a shadow of a representation, and that the government would be far less objectionable if the number and the expense were doubled. A patriot in a State that does not import or export finds insuperable objections to the power of direct taxation. The patriotic adversary in a State with great exports and imports is no less dissatisfied that the whole burden of taxes may be thrown on consumption. This politician discovers in the Constitution a direct and irresistible tendency to monarchy; that one is equally sure it will end in aristocracy. Another is puzzled to say which of these shapes it will finally take, but sees clearly that it must be one or the other. And a fourth is not lacking who, with no less confidence, affirms that the Constitution is so far from leaning toward either of these dangers that the weight on that side will not be enough to keep it upright and firm against its opposite tendencies. With another class of adversaries to the Constitution the language is that the legislative, executive and judiciary departments are intermixed in such a way as to contradict all ideas of regular government and all the precautions needed in favor of liberty. While this objection circulates in vague and general terms, few lend it their support. Let each one come forward with his own explanation, and scarcely any two are exactly agreed on the subject. In the eyes of one, the vicious part of the organization is the joining of the Senate with the President in the responsible function of appointing to offices, instead of vesting this executive power in the Executive alone. To another, the exclusion of the House of Representatives is equally offensive, since its numbers alone could be a proper security against corruption and bias in exercising such a power. For another, letting the President have any share in a power that must always be a dangerous engine in the hands of the chief executive is an unpardonable violation of the maxims of republican jealousy. According to some, no part of the arrangement is more inadmissible than trying impeachments before the Senate, which is alternately a member of both the legislative and executive departments, when this power so obviously belonged to the judiciary department. "We concur fully," others reply, "in the objection to this part of the plan, but we can never agree that a reference of impeachments to the judiciary authority would be an amendment of the error. Our principal dislike to the organization arises from the extensive powers already lodged in that department." Even among the zealous supporters of a council of state, the most irreconcilable disagreement is found over how it ought to be constituted. One gentleman demands that the council consist of a small number, to be appointed by the most numerous branch of the legislature. Another would prefer a larger number, and regards it as a fundamental condition that the appointment be made by the President himself.

Our argument can give no offense to the writers against the plan of the federal Constitution if we suppose that, as they are the most zealous, so they are also the wisest of those who think the recent Convention unequal to its assigned task, and that a wiser and better plan might and ought to be substituted. Let us suppose further that their country agrees, both with this favorable opinion of their merits and with their unfavorable opinion of the Convention, and so proceeds to form them into a second convention, with full powers and for the express purpose of revising and remolding the work of the first. Suppose the experiment were seriously made, though it takes some effort to view it seriously even as fiction. I leave it to be decided by the sample of opinions just displayed whether, with all their enmity toward their predecessors, they would depart from their example at any single point so widely as in the discord and ferment that would mark their own deliberations. I leave it also to be decided whether the Constitution now before the public would not stand as fair a chance of immortality as Lycurgus gave that of Sparta, by making its change depend on his own return from exile and death, if it were adopted immediately and were to remain in force, not until a BETTER one, but until ANOTHER should be agreed upon by this new assembly of lawgivers.

It is a matter of both wonder and regret that those who raise so many objections against the new Constitution never call to mind the defects of the one that is to be exchanged for it. The former need not be perfect; it is enough that the latter is more imperfect. No man would refuse to give brass for silver or gold because the silver or gold had some alloy in it. No man would refuse to leave a shattered and tottering house for a firm and comfortable building because the building had no porch, or because some of the rooms were a little larger or smaller, or the ceilings a little higher or lower, than he would have planned them. But setting aside illustrations of this sort, is it not plain that most of the main objections urged against the new system apply with tenfold weight against the existing Confederation? Is an unlimited power to raise money dangerous in the hands of the federal government? The present Congress can make requisitions, or formal requests for money, in any amount it pleases, and the States are constitutionally bound to furnish them. It can issue bills of credit as long as it will pay for the paper. It can borrow, abroad and at home, as long as a shilling will be lent. Is an unlimited power to raise troops dangerous? The Confederation gives Congress that power also, and Congress has already begun to use it. Is it improper and unsafe to mix the different powers of government in the same body of men? Congress, a single body of men, is the sole depositary of all the federal powers. Is it especially dangerous to put the keys of the treasury and the command of the army into the same hands? The Confederation places both in the hands of Congress. Is a bill of rights essential to liberty? The Confederation has no bill of rights. Is it an objection to the new Constitution that it empowers the Senate, with the concurrence of the Executive, to make treaties that are to be the laws of the land? The existing Congress, without any such check, can make treaties which it has itself declared, and most of the States have recognized, to be the supreme law of the land. Does the new Constitution permit the importation of slaves for twenty years? Under the old one it is permitted forever.

I shall be told that, however dangerous this mixture of powers may be in theory, it is made harmless by Congress's dependence on the States for the means of putting them into practice. However large the mass of powers may be, I shall be told, in fact it is a lifeless mass. To this I say, first, that the Confederation is then guilty of the still greater folly of declaring certain powers in the federal government absolutely necessary while at the same time making them absolutely worthless. I say, next, that if the Union is to continue and no better government is substituted, effective powers must either be granted to the existing Congress or be assumed by it, and in either case the contrast I have just drawn will hold good. But this is not all. Out of this lifeless mass an unnatural growth of power has already arisen, one that tends to realize every danger that can be feared from a defective construction of the supreme government of the Union. It is no longer a matter of speculation and hope that the Western territory is a mine of vast wealth to the United States. It is not of such a nature as to extricate them from their present distresses, or for some time to come to yield any regular supplies for the public expenses. Yet under proper management it must hereafter be able both to bring about a gradual discharge of the domestic debt and to furnish, for a certain period, liberal contributions to the federal treasury. A very large share of this fund has already been surrendered by individual States, and it may reasonably be expected that the remaining States will not persist in withholding similar proofs of their fairness and generosity. We may calculate, therefore, that a rich and fertile country, of an area equal to the inhabited extent of the United States, will soon become a national stock. Congress has taken over the administration of this stock. It has begun to make it productive. Congress has undertaken to do more. It has proceeded to form new States, to set up temporary governments, to appoint officers for them, and to prescribe the conditions on which such States shall be admitted into the Confederacy. All this has been done, and done without the least color of constitutional authority. Yet no blame has been whispered; no alarm has been sounded. A GREAT and INDEPENDENT fund of revenue is passing into the hands of a SINGLE BODY of men, who can RAISE TROOPS to an INDEFINITE NUMBER, and appropriate money for their support for an INDEFINITE PERIOD OF TIME. And yet there are men who have not only been silent spectators of this prospect but are advocates for the system that presents it, and who at the same time urge against the new system the objections we have heard. Would they not act more consistently if they urged the establishment of the new system as no less necessary to guard the Union against the future powers and resources of a body constructed like the existing Congress than to save it from the dangers threatened by that Assembly's present impotence?

By anything I have said here I do not mean to censure the measures Congress has pursued. I am aware that it could not have done otherwise. The public interest and the necessity of the case laid on it the task of overleaping its constitutional limits. But is not the fact an alarming proof of the danger that results from a government that lacks regular powers equal to its objects? Dissolution or usurpation is the dreadful dilemma to which such a government is continually exposed.
